blocks.text: But to this argument, which is drawn from the etymology, Michaelis in the Supplemm. vol. 3, p. 857 attributes little or nothing. "The name," he says, "can be derived from piety for several birds, and has been so derived, as for the vulture רחם from mercy, and for others, also here and there for חסידה; nor is this the only etymology offered by the oriental languages. For the חסידה, still unknown to us, could also be called from ܚܣܕܐ, disgrace, a foul bird; from the Arabic حسد [ḥasad], envious; from a marsh and a confluence of water [Michaelis no doubt has in view the Arabic حشد [ḥashada] he gathered, flowed together], marshy, dwelling in marshes. The lack of an etymology may be urged against some interpretations; none can be established by an etymology." So Michaelis, and rightly, as it seems to me. To this I add that piety is also celebrated in the heron, or herodius (see Aelian, Hist. Anim. book 3, ch. 23), the bird which the most ancient translators took for the Hebrew חסידה, as we saw in the preceding Chapter. Their interpretation can therefore be confirmed by this same etymology.

What Bochart adduces in the first place to prove that חסידה is the stork is this: Moses counts the chasida among the unclean birds and forbids the Jews to eat it, and this fits the stork especially well, since it feeds on serpents. But this reason for the prohibition fits many birds of the heron kind, which have this in common, that they feed on fish, frogs, serpents and aquatic insects. This argument, then, being too general, proves nothing.

This mixture of black and white in the colour of the feathers, too, the stork shares with many birds of the heron kind. Thus Aldrovandi, Ornithol. vol. 3, p. 377 f., on the Ardea cinerea, or the herodius of the ancients: "The upper neck, the whole back, likewise the wings, except the larger feathers, and also the tail are of an ash-grey colour. The flight feathers of the wings are blackish. The belly is white, as are also the breast and the lower neck, which are crossed by certain oblong black spots running downwards." The same on the second ash-grey heron, or the lesser, p. 380: "Among the black feathers of the crown others spring up that are white — — The wings are of a very handsome ash-grey colour, as is also the tail. But the neck in front and behind, the belly, the thighs and the underside of the tail are white." The same on the third kind of ash-grey heron, p. 383: "The feathers of the head, neck, back and upper wings are dusky from ash-grey, all marked at the tip with a reddish spot; those on the wings, which are rather larger, are variegated with white at the end, as are those that make up the tail. Those covering the breast are sprinkled with longer black, reddish and white markings. The belly is nearly white from ash-grey." You see, then, that this mark too is not so peculiar to the stork that another bird could not be thought of.

But this whole argument, which Bochart adduced in the second place, is just as uncertain as the one he put first. Of the first and second marks we have already seen that they are found in more than one bird of the heron kind. But the rest too, everything attributed to the bird חסידה in the Sacred codex, fits the ardea cinerea, or the ἐρωδιός [erōdios] of the Alexandrian translator, each and every point, no less than the stork. For both birds nest in trees (Ps. CIV, 17.), both are migratory (Ierem. VIII, 7.), and both, because of the swiftness of their flight, could be used as an image of the greatest speed (Zachar. V, 9.). Cf. Oedmann, Vermischte Sammlungen, fasc. 5, ch. 6, p. 64 ff., and Michaelis, Supplemm. vol. 3, p. 859, 860.

But Michaelis rightly warns, on Castell's Lexic. Syriac., edited by him, p. 320, and in the Supplemm. p. 859, that this authority of the most learned Maronites (who translated the Syriac version in the Polyglots into Latin) is nil; for they were accustomed to put under Syriac names of animals, trees and plants whose meanings they did not know the meanings that the common lexicons of their time gave for the Hebrew ones. Michaelis himself thinks it probable that the Syriac ܚܘܪܒܐ agrees with the Arabic خَرْبٌ [kharb], which Golius explains thus: the male of that bird whose whole kind is called حباري [ḥubārā], Hubara; which, as we saw above, is a species of otis or bustard.

Michaelis in the Supplemm. vol. 3, p. 858: „I do not deny it, especially since I learn from the travels of Ives that the stork is called Legleg by the Arabs. But what does this Arab, the translator of the prophets, matter here, who translated not the Hebrew but the Greek, in which at Zachar. V, 9. the name ἔποπος [epopos], of the hoopoe, is read? This could certainly have been called قعقع [qaʿqaʿ] in Arabic from the variety of its colour. In Jeremiah, indeed, Ἀσιδα [Asida] now stands; but since the translator renders it in the same way as in Zechariah, he seems also to have read the same. Be that as it may, the Arabic translator of the prophets is neither of such an age, nor of such skill in Hebrew letters, which he did not even read, that any authority resides in him.“
